- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

The official Figma MCP server. Use this server whenever the user wants to create, generate, edit, implement, or sync any design, UI, screen, component, mockup, or visual — in Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or Figma Slides — and whenever the user mentions Figma or provides a figma.com URL.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Write designs INTO Figma from code, intent, or existing components (use_figma, generate_figma_design, create_new_file, upload_assets)
- Bridge code and design via Code Connect (get_code_connect_map, add_code_connect_map)
- Create diagrams and FigJam content (generate_diagram, get_figjam)

- The user wants to create, mock up, or generate any UI, screen, component, or design — even if Figma isn't named
- The user wants to implement a design as code (design-to-code)
- The user wants to push a page, view, or component into Figma (code-to-design)
- The user wants to update, sync, or edit an existing Figma file
- The user shares a figma.com URL

Here are guidelines for using Supabase tools effectively:

- Before making schema changes, use `list_tables` to understand the existing structure
- When debugging issues, start with `get_logs` and `get_advisors` before making changes
- Use `get_project_url` and `get_publishable_api_key` when helping users configure client-side integrations

If you have access to a local development environment with a filesystem and shell:
- Install the Supabase agent skill for critical development and security guidance: `npx skills add supabase/agent-skills` (https://supabase.com/docs/guides/getting-started/ai-skills.md)
- Use the Supabase CLI (`supabase`) for local development workflows such as starting a local stack, managing migrations, and running edge functions locally (https://supabase.com/docs/guides/local-development.md)

If you are running in a web-only or remote environment without filesystem or shell access:

- implement: Pipeline completo de implementação: resolve o input (texto, plano ou link), garante um plano APROVADO via /refine, e dispara o workflow de implementação wave-based (agente fresco por onda + ledger persistente) que commita, verifica e abre o PR — com decisões autônomas documentadas. Ao final, auto-encadeia /review-fix-loop (desligável com 'no-review').
- refine: Transforma um pedido bruto (texto, arquivo de plano ou link — GitHub issue/PR, Jira, Slack) em um plano APROVADO com Contract block, decidindo sozinha se entrevista o usuário, se ilustra outcomes críticos para confirmação e se o risco exige /deep-plan antes da implementação. Substitui o plan mode interativo; usada isoladamente ou como etapa 1 do /implement.
- review-fix-loop: Loop review→fix em contexto limpo sobre um PR aberto: revisa (espelho da GitHub Action de code review da Anthropic, ou deep-review com 8 lentes + enumeração de facetas quando a mudança é complexa/money/deep-planned), concilia com comentários e reviews já postados no PR, posta o review consolidado no GitHub, e um agente fixer endereça os pontos (commit+push, atualiza descrição, responde quando diverge). Round 1 em largura, rounds seguintes em profundidade (validador + fix-diff + re-enumeração); repete até exaustão — 0 High/Blocker em round de largura com enumeração seca (cap 5 rounds) — + uma rodada final para Medium/Low.
- deep-plan: Planning-time mirror of deep-review: fills and adversarially refutes a plan-contract (interaction matrix, dimension table, precondition diff) from design intent + the live codebase, before code exists. Auto-engages in plan mode for sensitive-domain status/lifecycle/flow-replacement changes; self-tiers to a light inline pass for trivial or non-sensitive plans.
- deep-review: Perform a thorough code review using parallel domain-specialized agents and core business tenets. Accepts a PR number/URL, branch name, commit SHA, or reviews current local changes by default.
- verify: Run after any code change. Runs the repo's configured format/lint/build/test pipeline with a fix loop until it's green, then reports honestly. Use when the user asks to verify, build, run tests, or confirm a change is sound — and proactively after editing code.
- verify-plan: Reconcile an implementation against the plan that specified it — flags dropped commitments (coverage), changed predicates/values (fidelity), and unplanned logic (scope-creep). Cheap, plan-grounded; run before opening a PR or per-commit during long implementations. Not a bug hunt — use /deep-review for emergent-interaction coverage.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

{"body":"Part of #35 (section 3, enhancement 8 + section 4 behavioural notes). Depends on #46 (paint tooling). Resolves three of #35's open questions — decisions recorded below.

## The gap

After the tile runtime and paint tool land, autotile rules still live as **DSL strings in code**: changing "which art goes on a dirt cell whose top and left face air" means editing a C# string and rebuilding. The artist's iteration loop runs through a programmer.

## The design (proven in the game)

**The Autotile Rules WORKSPACE** — a full-screen view, not a panel:
- one rule set per `TilePaintValue`, `+ New Rule Set…`;
- the 16 exposure cases shown **visually**, with a toggle to the raw DSL string for power users;
- `Change Tileset…` binding picker;
- edits are **LIVE and undoable** (`PaintValueEditCommand`) — no Save/Cancel; every change immediately re-bakes the visible world, so real terrain re-dresses as you adjust a rule, and Ctrl+Z takes it back. Editing rules stops being programming and becomes painting.

**Workspaces** — the rules editor is a different *activity*, so the window top bar gains Blender-style tabs (`Level Editor` / `Autotile Rules`, `EditorShellStateComponent.ActiveWorkspace`), with Undo/Redo/Refresh right-anchored.

## Decisions (approved by the maintainer in #35's follow-up)

1. **Workspaces stay hardcoded-two.** A registry serving two fixed entries is speculative generality; the third workspace, whenever it exists, pays for the mechanical refactor. Recorded here so that refactor has a paper trail.
2. **`EditorChromeBuilder.DefaultButtons` loses the collider verbs — adopted.** They move to the entity context menu under `Collider ▸`: those verbs act on the SELECTION (contextual), while top-level chrome holds app-level verbs (undo, refresh, workspace tabs). ⚠️ Behavioural change for existing consumers — fewer default toolbar buttons; nothing removed, relocated. Must be flagged prominently in the PR notes.
3. **The 944-line interior read**: the divergence analysis verified `AutotileRuleEditorSystem`'s API surface, module boundaries and absence of game terms, but not every line. The full line-read happens during PR preparation, findings recorded in the PR description, so review starts from an audited base.

## Delivery

- [ ] Port `System/AutotileRuleEditorSystem.cs` (944 lines — full read at PR prep, per decision 3), `System/WorkspaceTabStripSystem.cs` (260), `Undo/PaintValueCommands.cs`
- [ ] Wiring: `EditorShellStateComponent` (`EditorWorkspace`), `UI/EditorChromeLayout.cs`, `UI/EditorChromeBuilder.cs` (decision 2), `EditorContextMenuModel` (`Collider ▸` submenu), `EditorOverlay`
- [ ] Premises entry: workspaces; live undoable rule edits
- [ ] Test: a rule edit re-bakes visibly and undoes; rule-set CRUD round-trips serialization; workspace switch preserves both views' state; collider verbs reachable via the context menu

Reference implementation: `roo-oliv/gmtk-2026gj` → `Gmtk2026.Core/MonoDreams/level-editor/…`

**Value on its own:** the autotile system becomes artist-editable with live feedback — the difference between a feature programmers can use and one teams can.
","comments":[],"labels":[],"title":"level-editor: workspaces + live autotile rules editor (collider verbs move to the context menu)"}

38	  `EditorThemeLintTests` on main itself (found 2026-08-05 while gating #50 — the reference has no

45	  ported into `PaintValueCommands.cs`). Local ADDED the locked-layer loud refusal the ref lacks.

49	  legitimate break; update the facts in the same PR.

description: "How to port waves from the gmtk-2026gj reference repo for issues #45-#57 (the #35 upstreaming batch)"
metadata:

Issues #45–#57 (the #35 "Upstreaming Witch v Necromancer" batch) port waves from
`roo-oliv/gmtk-2026gj` → `Gmtk2026.Core/MonoDreams/<module>/…` (host-screen wiring lives in
`Gmtk2026.Core/Screens/GameplayScreen.cs`). What worked for #48 (PR #71, 2026-08-05):

- Shallow-clone the reference into the scratchpad and **diff file-by-file** against the local
  module — the reference has ALL waves interleaved, so scope by issue: TileGrid/paint = #45/#46,
  workspaces/autotile/collider-menu = #47, layers panel + HUD preview = #48 (done),
  pixel-art asset loop (IHDR auto-grid, .anim cards, file: ladder) = #49 (done, PR #74,
  2026-08-07 — a full local clone already sits at ~/git/roo-oliv/gmtk-2026gj, no need to
  re-clone; the in-scope hunks of PalettePlacementSystem/EditorOverlay excluded the Paint-tab
  wave cleanly).
- Some "port items" already landed with earlier issues (the SceneLayer serializer shipped with
  #44) — verify before porting.
- The reference ships NO tests and has latent bugs (its Eye/EyeOff glyph geometry escapes the
  icon rect; MonoDreams' `EditorIconsTests` geometry lint catches it). Author tests fresh from
  the issue's test list; don't trust the reference blindly.
- Two parallel coding agents in one worktree: only ONE may run dotnet (obj/ lock races — see
  [[verify-gate-gotchas]]); the other verifies APIs by reading source. Have both RETURN premises
  text instead of editing premises.md (merge conflicts); the orchestrator integrates.
- Agents' `dotnet restore` can churn `MonoDreams/packages.lock.json` (KNI packages promoted to
  Direct) — revert before committing.
- Sibling-wave PRs collide in the same files (`PalettePlacementSystem`, `premises.md`) — on rebase
  the auto-merge tends to CONVERGE on the reference's shape (it has all waves combined), so verify
  the merged hot spots against the reference file, not against either parent (#50's `StampAt` came
  out byte-identical to the ref after rebasing over #48's layers wave).
- The waves can also break EACH OTHER's lint gates on main: #48's tile-grid merge put
  `TileGridBakeSystem.cs` (raw `Color.White`×5) inside `level-editor`, tripping
  `EditorThemeLintTests` on main itself (found 2026-08-05 while gating #50 — the reference has no
  such lint). Check whether a red gate is pre-existing on origin/main before debugging your branch.

#46 (PR #76, 2026-08-07) additions — divergences #47's rebase will collide with:
- Local DROPPED the ref's write-only `EditorBottomTab.Paint` + `panel:tab paint` op (dead state — the
  paint shelf is ACTIVE-layer-driven), the paint system's unused `createDefaults` ctor param + its
  stale "PaintGrid auto-creation" doc, and `PaintValueEditCommand` (only `AddPaintValueCommand`
  ported into `PaintValueCommands.cs`). Local ADDED the locked-layer loud refusal the ref lacks.
- Ref's `ReflectState` swatch uses lint-illegal `new Color(...)` — the theme lint blesses only
  target-typed `new(...)`; route swatches through a target-typed local.
- Menu-shape tests (`EditorContextMenuTests`) assert exact item counts — adding a menu item is a
  legitimate break; update the facts in the same PR.
- Background `dotnet test ... | tail` masks the exit code (pipe exit wins) — grep the output for
  `Com falha!`/`Aprovado!`, never trust exit 0 through a pipe.

**Why:** the same porting motion repeats for every sibling issue in the batch.
**How to apply:** clone reference → diff → scope by issue number → parallel agents (one builds) →
full Release gate → premises → PR with `Closes #N`.

1	# MonoDreams — Core Tenets
2	
3	> The invariants and design principles that hold across the engine.
4	> Read this before working on MonoDreams — most of what looks surprising in
5	> the code is consistent with one of these tenets. AI coding agents should
6	> load this file as context for any non-trivial task in the repo.
7	
8	## 1. Framework, not library
9	
10	MonoDreams is to game devs what Spring is to web devs: the framework owns
11	the heavy lifting (rendering, camera, physics, level loading, spawning),
12	the developer owns the gameplay code, and the price of full control is
13	embracing ECS. The competitive position is between **bare MonoGame** (too
14	low-level — you write the rendering loop yourself) and **Nez or similar**
15	(too loose — you give up control to get convenience).
16	
17	**Two users, equal weight.**
18	- Solo devs and small indie teams who *like writing code* and want plug'n
19	  play primitives.
20	- AI coding agents (Claude Code and similar) operating on the codebase.
21	  Docs in this repo — CORE_TENETS, premises files, CLAUDE.md — are
22	  first-class context for that user, not human-only supplementary material.
23	
24	**Key rule.** When choosing between a more specialized API and a more
25	general one, pick the general one. The same primitive should serve more
26	than one feature; if it can't, it's probably a game-shaped abstraction
27	hiding inside the framework.
28	
29	## 2. ECS purity & composition
30	
31	The architecture is composition all the way down:
32	
33	- **Components** are pure data containers. No logic, no methods beyond
34	  trivial property getters. If you reach for a method on a component, the
35	  logic belongs in a system.
36	- **Systems** are pure functions over components. A system declares the
37	  components it operates on and acts on every entity that matches. It
38	  makes **no assumption** about which other systems ran before or will
39	  run after.
40	- **Entities** are IDs that group components. They carry no state of
41	  their own.
42	- **The pipeline assembler — the screen — owns ordering.** The screen
43	  registers systems in the order they should run for that screen's
44	  intended behavior. A system that quietly depends on another system
45	  having run is a framework-level bug; the dependency belongs in the
46	  pipeline assembly, not inside the system.
47	
48	**Atomic unit of composition.** A new feature usually lands as one or
49	more new systems, sometimes paired with one new component. Components
50	are added only when there is genuinely new data to model. Net: the engine
51	should always have more systems than components.
52	
53	**Discover before creating.** Before adding a component or system,
54	search what's already there. Prefer extending an existing component to
55	creating a new one (CLAUDE.md says the same — it is repeated here because
56	this is the most common review finding). The failure mode is a plethora
57	of micro-components, each solving one feature's narrow pain, none
58	reusable.
59	
60	**Key invariant.** Public contracts — messages, components, public
61	systems — must be backed by a test or example that exercises them.
62	Contracts without a maintained use site become indistinguishable from
63	dead code, and the framework cannot signal "this is part of the API" by
64	name alone.
65	
66	**Key rule (the #1 review lens).** When a PR adds a new component or
67	system, ask: *does this evolve well as more features land, or did we
68	just solve today's pain?* A hyper-specialized addition that doesn't
69	generalize is the framework's primary failure mode. If a generalization
70	isn't obvious, propose extending an existing primitive instead.
71	
72	### Aspirational direction
73	
74	- **Declarative system dependencies.** Today, ordering is implicit in
75	  the screen's registration order. A future API would let a system
76	  declare "I expect X to have run this frame" and let the framework
77	  enforce or warn at registration time.
78	- **Modular packs.** Today the engine is one bundle. The intended
79	  end-state is Spring-style modules (`MonoDreams.Rendering`,
80	  `MonoDreams.Physics`, `MonoDreams.Dialogue`, …) that can be adopted
81	  independently. The current `MonoDreams.YarnSpinner/` is the
82	  closest prototype.
83	- **Test or example per public contract.** New messages, components, and
84	  systems should ship with at least one usage that proves the contract
85	  works and signals that it's maintained.
86	
87	## 3. Hierarchy & Transform
88	
89	`Transform` is the engine's spatial component today. It holds position,
90	rotation, scale, origin, and an optional parent link; it caches a world
91	matrix and exposes `WorldPosition` / `WorldRotation` / `WorldScale`
92	properties that walk the parent chain.
93	
94	**Key invariant — don't mix two Transform-shaped components in one
95	project.** A developer is free to write a `MyTransform` with different
96	trade-offs; what breaks the framework is **mixing** `Transform` and
97	`MyTransform` in the same world. Systems should be agnostic enough to
98	operate on either one (see §2 — systems are functions), but the bundled
99	collision, rendering, camera, and culling systems read `Transform`
100	specifically. Using a custom transform means re-implementing those
101	consumers too.
102	
103	**Two parent links, intentionally.** `Transform.Parent` is the matrix
104	link (it determines how `WorldMatrix` cascades); `ChildOf` is a
105	structural marker (it determines lifecycle and cascading disposal). The
106	split exists to support complex hierarchical UI such as a dialogue
107	panel — a single visual whose banner, avatars, text and waiting-indicator
108	move and dispose together but may not all share matrix scaling.
109	`HierarchySystem` keeps the two in sync. **This split is on the refactor
110	backlog** (§10); read both fields when reasoning about hierarchy until it
111	is consolidated.
112	
113	**Dirty propagation.** Mutating a parent's transform marks the entire
114	descendant chain dirty; `WorldMatrix` is a cached property whose getter
115	re-walks the chain when needed. Systems that read `WorldPosition` get
116	the parent-corrected value, but only if `HierarchySystem` has run in the
117	pipeline ahead of them — that's the pipeline assembler's job to arrange.
118	
119	**`Transform.Delta` and `HasMoved`.** These reflect the change between
120	two committed positions. They are meaningful only after
121	`TransformCommitSystem` has run for the *previous* frame. Today no API
122	prevents reading stale `Delta` mid-frame; this is on the backlog as
123	"`Transform` should expose interaction methods that guarantee `Delta`
124	consistency" (§10). For now, downstream systems that depend on `Delta`
125	(notably the collision detection's swept tests) must trust the
126	assembler put `TransformCommitSystem` at the end of every frame.
127	
128	### Aspirational direction
129	
130	Collision, rendering, culling, and camera all read `Transform`
131	directly. The intended end-state is loose coupling — those modules
132	operate against any *Transform-shaped contract*, so a developer can
133	swap in `MyTransform` without re-implementing them. The framework
134	currently doesn't enforce this; treat any `MonoDreams/System/`
135	reference to `Transform` as implementation debt rather than design.
136	
137	## 4. Rendering pipeline
138	
139	The rendering pipeline is the most delicate part of the engine. Bugs
140	here are visual rather than logical, which makes them harder to debug
141	than crashes. Two rules cover most of the surface:
142	
143	**Key invariant — `DrawComponent` is the unified render component.**
144	There is one `DrawComponent` per renderable entity. Its `Type` field is
145	one of `Sprite`, `Text`, `NinePatch`, or `Mesh`, mutually exclusive.
146	Source data lives in companion structs (`SpriteInfo`, `DynamicText`,
147	`NinePatchInfo`, mesh buffers) populated by prep systems
148	(`SpritePrepSystem`, `TextPrepSystem`, `MeshPrepSystem`).
149	**Do not create new draw/render components.** Adding a new visual type
150	extends `DrawElementType` and `MasterRenderSystem`; it does not fork
151	the pipeline.
152	
153	**Key invariant — `MasterRenderSystem` is the sole renderer.** No game
154	code should call `SpriteBatch` outside the prep-then-master path. A
155	parallel render system is a framework violation — flagged by review.
156	
157	**Key rule — rendering systems run last.** In any pipeline assembly,
158	the prep-cull-sort-render module goes at the end. The recommended order
159	inside the module, from the reference assembly
160	(`LoadLevelExampleGameScreen.cs:277–331`), is:
161	`CullingSystem` → `SpritePrepSystem` → `YSortSystem` → `TextPrepSystem`
162	→ `MeshPrepSystem` → `MasterRenderSystem`.
163	
164	**Render targets.** Three are defined by `RenderTargetID`:
165	- **Main** — world-space, camera transform applied, **respects culling**.
166	- **UI** — screen-space, no camera transform, always renders.
167	- **HUD** — screen-space, no camera transform, always renders.
168	
169	The `Visible` tag is added and removed by `CullingSystem` based on the
170	camera's `VirtualScreenBounds`. Only the Main target consults it. UI and
171	HUD entities don't need `Visible`; if you put a `Visible`-gated entity
172	on UI by mistake, it will always render (which is usually the desired
173	outcome anyway — but the failure mode is the reverse: a Main-target
174	entity that never gets `Visible` because no `CullingSystem` is in the
175	pipeline, and the dev stares at an invisible sprite). The renderable
176	entity stack is therefore `EntityInfo + Transform + SpriteInfo +
177	DrawComponent + Visible` for Main, minus `Visible` for UI/HUD.
178	**This split is a known wart** (§10): `Visible` may become a property of
179	`DrawComponent` to remove the easy-to-miss tag.
180	
181	**Layer depth ownership.** Three systems write `LayerDepth` — four when a
182	screen composes scene layers — in this order: `SpritePrepSystem`
183	initializes it from the sprite's layer, the optional `SceneLayerSystem`
184	remaps each scene-layer member's depth from (layer order, within-layer
185	key) while entities on no layer pass through untouched (see §6),
186	`YSortSystem` may override it for entities on Y-sorted layers, and
187	`MasterRenderSystem` sorts on the final value. `YSortSystem` uses a
188	minimal epsilon to bias parent-child groups so children stay attached
189	to their parent's depth band. Same-layer entities with the same world Y
190	fall through to insertion order — no other tiebreaker exists; if
191	flicker becomes a problem, that's where to look.
192	
193	**Camera.** A `Camera` instance owns its virtual resolution
194	(immutable after construction) and exposes mutable zoom, position, and
195	rotation. Multiple cameras at once are explicitly supported — local
196	multiplayer or CCTV-style views. `CameraFollowSystem` is *optional*:
197	fixed-camera games or custom camera systems are valid; just don't
198	register `CameraFollowSystem` and `CullingSystem` will still read
199	whatever the `Camera` reports.
200	
201	## 5. Physics & collision
202	
203	The framework provides Newtonian-style movement, gravity, layer-based
204	collision filtering, and AABB plus convex-polygon (SAT) collision
205	detection. These pieces are independent components and systems — a
206	game can use velocity without collision, or collision without
207	gravity — and the pipeline assembler picks which to register.
208	
209	**Components.** `Velocity` carries current and last velocity vectors
210	(the delta is exposed); `RigidBody` carries mass, gravity participation,
211	kinematic flag, and freeze-axis flags. A collider is its OWN entity now
212	(colliders-as-entities): `BoxCollider` carries a centered `Size`
213	(no offset — pose comes from the collider entity's `Transform`) and
214	active layers; `ConvexCollider` carries collider-entity-local vertices,
215	world-space vertices, a broadphase AABB and active layers. `ColliderTag`
216	is auto-applied to any collider entity so detection queries can match a
217	unified tag. A collider's **body** (the entity a contact acts on) is
218	resolved via `ColliderBody.Resolve` — nearest `RigidBody`/`Velocity`
219	ancestor, else itself — and `CollisionMessage` carries both the collider
220	entities and their bodies; resolution writes corrections to the body.
221	
222	**The reference physics pipeline order**, from
223	`LoadLevelExampleGameScreen.cs:277–286`:
224	**Movement → Velocity → Detection → Resolution → Commit.**
225	Each stage owns one job:
226	- *Movement* — game systems write `Velocity` based on input and AI.
227	- *Velocity (`VelocitySystem`)* — apply `Velocity` to `Transform.Position`.
228	- *Detection (`TransformCollisionDetectionSystem`)* — broadphase via AABB
229	  + narrowphase via SAT for `ConvexCollider`; emit `CollisionMessage`s.
230	- *Resolution (`TransformCollisionResolutionSystem` or
231	  `TransformPhysicalCollisionResolutionSystem`)* — correct positions and
232	  velocities for contacts; honor `RigidBody` freeze flags.
233	- *Commit (`TransformCommitSystem`)* — finalize `LastPosition`, so the
234	  next frame's `Delta` is meaningful.
235	
236	Swept collision (the dynamic AABB-vs-AABB and convex-vs-convex tests)
237	reads `Transform.Delta`. Delta is correct only if the previous frame
238	ended with `TransformCommitSystem`. Skip `Commit` and collisions go
239	through walls — see §3.
240	
241	**`ConvexCollider.BroadPhaseAABB`.** This AABB must be refreshed when
242	the world vertices change (transform moved or rotated). Detection
243	filters on it; a stale AABB makes a real collision invisible to the
244	broadphase. The detection system updates it; if you write a system
245	that mutates a convex collider's vertices directly, refresh the
246	broadphase AABB before the next detection pass.
247	
248	**Single-threaded detection.** `TransformCollisionDetectionSystem`
249	holds instance-level polygon buffers. It is intentionally not
250	thread-safe; do not register two instances or invoke it from parallel
251	contexts.
252	
253	**Multiple colliders per body (colliders-as-entities).** A collider is its
254	own entity, so a body owns N collider children — the former
255	one-collider-of-each-type-per-entity assumption is retired. Detection
256	iterates collider entities; resolution corrects each contact's body,
257	accumulating sequentially with per-message re-validation so a body hit
258	through two of its colliders in one frame is not double-corrected. Two
259	shape components on ONE entity is still not a thing (it would be a single
260	collider entity with an ambiguous shape) — give each shape its own child
261	collider entity.
262	
263	### Aspirational direction
264	
265	Collision is currently coupled to `Transform` (see §3). The intended
266	end-state is collision against any Transform-shaped contract.
267	
268	## 6. Level loading & entity spawning
269	
270	**The shipped game boots native `.mdscene` levels only** (see "Native-only
271	load" below). The LDtk (`.ldtk`) module is now **import-only**: its loader and
272	parsers run once, off the game boot, to migrate a legacy level into a native
273	scene the game then owns. The pipeline below describes that **import** path — a
274	request loads a file, the parser walks the data, and it emits
275	`EntitySpawnRequest` messages that a factory turns into entities. It is
276	composed only in the reference screen's `importMode`, never at live boot.
277	
278	**The pipeline.**
279	1. Game code publishes `LoadLevelRequest`.
280	2. The import composition registers **`level-ldtk`'s own
281	   `LDtkLevelLoadSystem`** as the handler for that message (in place of the
282	   native-only `LevelLoadRequestSystem` the boot path composes). It loads the
283	   LDtk file and **adds `LDtkLevelDataComponent` to the world** — the LDtk
284	   module's own level singleton, carrying the full `LDtkLevel` — plus the
285	   format-agnostic `CurrentLevelComponent(identifier)` marker and the
286	   background color.
287	3. The LDtk parsers (`LDtkEntityParserSystem`, `LDtkTileParserSystem`)
288	   **subscribe to `LDtkLevelDataComponent` being added** and parse on add.
289	4. Parsers emit `EntitySpawnRequest`s. Layer-derived data they can no longer
290	   pass as an LDtk type rides `CustomFields` under the `ldtk:` keys of
291	   `LDtkSpawnFields`.
292	5. `EntitySpawnSystem` consumes each spawn request and dispatches to an
293	   `IEntityFactory` registered for the request's string identifier.
294	
295	**Key invariant — `level-loading` is format-agnostic; the dependency arrow
296	points parser → plumbing.** No LDtk type appears in `level-loading` source
297	(issue #54): the shared `CurrentLevelComponent` holds a plain string
298	identifier, `EntitySpawnRequest` has no `LayerInstance` member, and
299	`LevelLoadRequestSystem` has no `ContentManager` and no format fallback.
300	Everything format-shaped lives in the format's own module — its level
301	component, its `LoadLevelRequest` handler, and its namespaced `CustomFields`
302	keys. A game that never installs `level-ldtk` therefore never compiles
303	against LDtk. When you add a format, add a module; do not add a branch or a
304	typed member to the shared plumbing.
305	
306	**Key invariant — the parsers react to component lifecycle, not
307	to push messages.** Their pattern (subscribe to their module's level
308	component being added) is the engine-wide default. A test or tool that sets
309	`LDtkLevelDataComponent` manually triggers them just as well as the regular
310	`LoadLevelRequest` path — and without a content pipeline. For new parsers,
311	follow this pattern — resist the urge to make a system "only respond when the
312	right message arrived"; that couples the system to an upstream sequence that
313	should be the assembler's choice.
314	
315	**Factory registration.** `EntitySpawnSystem` keeps a dictionary of
316	`string → IEntityFactory`. Game code registers factories at screen
317	setup time. Currently, an unregistered identifier produces a logged
318	warning and the spawn is silently dropped. **Intended behavior is to
319	throw** — this is on the backlog (§10). For now, treat the warning as a
320	high-severity signal during development.
321	
322	**Native-only load — the content-driven unification (PS5, asymmetry
323	resolved).** `LevelLoadRequestSystem` is now a **native-only** dispatcher:
324	each `LoadLevelRequest` probes for a bundled native scene
325	`Content/Levels/<id>.mdscene` via `TitleContainer` (the console-portable
326	read) and, on a hit, loads it through the generalized `SceneReaderSystem`
327	(the same native reader the editor's `LoadSceneRequest` uses —
328	reconstructing entities from serialized components, not factories). An id
329	with **no** native scene **fails loud** — there is no LDtk branch in the system
330	to fall back to (issue #54 removed it along with the `ContentManager`).
331	Native `.mdscene` is the game's real level format: versioned in
332	`Content/Levels/`, MGCB-`/copy:`-bundled, read read-only via `TitleContainer`
333	on every platform (only the desktop editor writes, PS3). **The whole LDtk module
334	is now IMPORT-ONLY machinery:** its loader + parsers run once — via the import op
335	(a headless `--export-scene <id>` / `MONODREAMS_EXPORT_SCENE` dev op, or a future
336	editor toolbar action) — to re-parse a legacy level and serialize the resulting
337	world to a native `.mdscene` the game then owns; they are **not wired to live
338	game boot** (composed only in the reference screen's `importMode`, which
339	registers `LDtkLevelLoadSystem` in place of `LevelLoadRequestSystem`). This
340	closes the parser-asymmetry backlog (§10): one content-driven load path.
341	(The Blender importer that once shared this path was retired in wave BR —
342	see §10.) Migration status: the committed
343	`Content/Levels/Blender_Level.mdscene` (a native scene originally migrated
344	from Blender) boots native; the LDtk `Level_0` is not yet migrated (its
345	~21k per-tile entities need a native tile-layer batching primitive — a
346	follow-up, §10).
347	
348	## 7. The reference pipeline
349	
350	`LoadLevelExampleGameScreen.cs:277–331` is the gold-standard pipeline
351	assembly. Read it before composing a new screen. The recommended
352	overall order, end-to-end:
353	
354	1. **Input** — keyboard/mouse polling, `InputReplaySystem` if running
355	   under replay.
356	2. **Game logic** — game-specific systems that read input and entity
357	   state to update gameplay components (movement intent, AI decisions,
358	   dialogue state).
359	3. **Physics module** — `MovementSystem` → `VelocitySystem` →
360	   `TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` →
361	   `TransformCollisionResolutionSystem` (or `…PhysicalCollisionResolutionSystem`) →
362	   `TransformCommitSystem`.
363	4. **Hierarchy** — `HierarchySystem` (then `TransformCommitSystem` if
364	   children moved independently), `SizeSystem`, `LayoutSystem`.
365	5. **Camera** — `CameraFollowSystem` (optional).
366	6. **Cursor** — `CursorInputSystem`, `CursorPositionSystem`.
367	7. **Render module** — `CullingSystem` → `SpritePrepSystem` →
368	   `YSortSystem` → `TextPrepSystem` → `MeshPrepSystem` →
369	   `MasterRenderSystem` → debug overlays.
370	
371	Each game's screen owns its own pipeline. The reference assembly is a
372	recommendation — fixed-camera games omit `CameraFollowSystem`,
373	non-physics screens skip the physics module, UI-only screens may have
374	no game logic at all. What does not change is the *shape* of the order:
375	input first, render last, with physics ahead of hierarchy and hierarchy
376	ahead of culling.
377	
378	### Aspirational direction
379	
380	A declarative system-dependencies API would let
381	`TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` say "I need `VelocitySystem` before
382	me this frame" and let the framework validate the assembly. Until that
383	exists, ordering bugs are caught by review (see the `/deep-review`
384	skill at §`.claude/skills/deep-review/SKILL.md`) and by behaviour
385	tests.
386	
387	## 8. Debug & testing
388	
389	The engine provides a small set of debug primitives. They are
390	*available*, not *required* — most screens register none of them.
391	
392	**`Logger`.** A static, lock-protected singleton in
393	`MonoDreams.State.Logger`. `Initialize(outputDirectory)` must be called
394	once before use; `Shutdown()` must be called to flush. Output goes to
395	`<dir>/monodreams_<timestamp>.log` with format `[wallclock] [GT gametime]
396	[LEVEL] message`. Replaces `Console.WriteLine`. The `MONODREAMS_DEBUG_DIR`
397	environment variable redirects all debug output (logs, replay input,
398	screenshots) for test isolation.
399	
400	**Input replay.** Drop `debug/input_replay.json` in the build output
401	directory. Format: `{ startLevel, description, commands: [{ action, type,
402	time }] }`. Actions match `AInputState` names. The `startLevel` field
403	skips menus and jumps straight into the named game screen. The game
404	auto-exits when the replay finishes.
405	
406	**Frame capture.** `ScreenshotCaptureSystem` writes frames to the debug
407	directory in one of two formats: PNG (encoded off-thread; the right
408	choice for occasional verification shots, but the ~50 ms encode caps a
409	per-frame capture at ~15–26 fps) or raw RGBA (`CaptureFormat.Raw` — a
410	synchronous memcpy dump sustaining full frame rate, ~3.5 MiB per frame
411	at 1280x720). Off by default. Env-driven capture goes through
412	`ScreenshotCaptureSystem.FromEnvironment`, the single owner of the
413	`MONODREAMS_SCREENSHOT=1|png|raw` / `MONODREAMS_SCREENSHOT_INTERVAL` /
414	`MONODREAMS_SCREENSHOT_MAX_FRAMES` contract; the replay-gated pattern
415	(`"screenshots": true` in `input_replay.json`) still drives
416	PNG-interval capture. See the `debug` module's `docs/overview.md`
417	§ Frame capture for the disk-cost table and the raw-vs-encoded
418	rationale.
419	
420	**Headless mode — two hosts, two contracts.** There are two headless
421	paths and they do *not* do the same thing:
422	
423	- **Examples** (`dotnet run --project MonoDreams.Examples -- --headless`)
424	  creates a 1×1 off-screen window and **early-returns from `Draw`** — it
425	  runs Update-side logic at max speed but renders **nothing**. It is
426	  convenient for fast logic/replay integration tests via `GameTestRunner`
427	  but cannot observe any visual or render-path behaviour. Treat it as the
428	  logic-only path; don't rely on it for rendering correctness.
429	- **Demos** (`dotnet run --project MonoDreams.Demos -- --headless --screen
430	  <name> --frames <N> --exit`) is the **observe-and-self-verify** path
431	  (issue #28). It keeps a real `GraphicsDevice` on a hidden, full-virtual-
432	  resolution backbuffer, **renders every frame** (`Draw` is not a no-op),
433	  dumps non-blank PNGs to `MONODREAMS_DEBUG_DIR`, logs periodic live-heap
434	  samples, and self-terminates after `<N>` frames. This is the supported
435	  way for an agent to verify its own work on the demo host without a human.
436	  See the `debug` module premises ("Headless Demos renders every frame";
437	  "Headless heap samples measure the live set") and
438	  `MonoDreams.Tests/IntegrationTests/HeadlessDemoTests.cs`.
439	
440	A literal zero-window mode / null `GraphicsDevice` is **not** possible on
441	MonoGame DesktopGL 3.8.4 (the window hosts the GL context); a hidden
442	window that never presents is the achievable form of "headless render".
443	
444	**Testing.** `MonoDreams.Tests/` uses xUnit + the custom
445	`GameTestRunner`, which spawns the game in headless mode with a temp
446	debug directory, writes an `InputReplayPlan`, waits for exit, and
447	exposes log-assertion helpers (`AssertLogContains`,
448	`AssertLogContainsInOrder`, `GetLogLines`). The gold-standard tests
449	today are `SATCollisionTests` (pure-logic), `BlenderLevelTests`
450	(native scene boot), and `InfiniteRunnerTests` (integration).
451	
452	**No architectural tests today.** ArchUnit-style assertions
453	("`MonoDreams/Component/*.cs` must contain only data") do not exist
454	yet. Most premises in `docs/{domain}/premises.md` start their `Tests:`
455	field as `none yet`; introducing architectural tests is on the backlog.
456	
457	## 9. The editor is part of the game
458	
459	The level editor is **not a separate application** and **not a separate
460	renderer** — it is the running game under an editor run configuration.
461	There is one world, one `Camera`, and one draw stack
462	(`CullingSystem → SpritePrepSystem → YSortSystem → MeshPrepSystem →
463	TextPrepSystem → MasterRenderSystem`); the editor previews exactly what
464	the player sees because it runs that same pipeline. What changes between
465	playing and editing is not *which* pipeline runs but *which systems in
466	it are allowed to run* — a **run-state contract** the engine codifies in
467	`foundation` — and the run state is driven by a **transport**, not a
468	mode-toggle key.
469	
470	**The transport model.** Under the editor run flag (`--editor` /
471	`MONODREAMS_EDITOR=1` — the ONLY way into the editor) the shell, chrome,
472	and editor systems are **always composed and visible**; no key toggles
473	the editor away. The designer drives the game like a media player through
474	the toolbar's left-most transport buttons (or the headless
475	`Play`/`Pause`/`Restart` editor ops), owned by `EditorTransport`:
476	**Paused** = `RunMode.Edit` (game logic Freeze-gated, editing tools
477	live — the boot state under the flag), **Playing** = `RunMode.Play`
478	(the game runs inside the inset viewport; the shell stays up and the
479	transport buttons + systems panel stay interactive, but the editing
480	tools are inert — a click in the viewport belongs to the game), and
481	**Restart** = return the world to the state of the original load:
482	clear the undo history, remove the world-level **marker** components
483	(`CurrentLevelComponent` — a plain string level id now — and
484	`CurrentBackgroundColorComponent`, so the reload starts from a clean
485	world-level state; a `Set` over a still-present component fires *Changed*, not
486	*Added*. The LDtk parsers key off `level-ldtk`'s own `LDtkLevelDataComponent`,
487	which exists only in the import-op composition — where the transport never
488	runs — so it is deliberately not swept), dispose every scene entity (editor infrastructure — entities tagged
489	`EditorInfrastructureComponent` — the cursor pipeline, and
490	screen-`KeepAlive`-named infrastructure survive), re-run the screen's
491	recorded `Reload`, and land Paused. **Unsaved live edits are discarded
492	by Restart** — the standard play-mode trade-off; Save first to keep
493	them.
494	
495	**The run-state contract.** `GameState.RunMode` is one of `Play`
496	(default) or `Edit`. A system opts into run-state awareness by being
497	wrapped in a `GatedSystem` carrying an `EditTimeBehavior` policy
498	(`RunNormally` / `Freeze` / `RunPartial` / `RuntimeEditable`). Each
499	frame the gate reads `RunMode` and decides whether to forward to its
500	child: `RunNormally` runs in both modes; `Freeze` runs in `Play` only;
501	`RunPartial` and `RuntimeEditable` are reserved (today they run in both,
502	finer semantics deferred). Editor tooling is **ECS systems over this
503	gated game pipeline** — selection, gizmo, undo-apply, scene save/load,
504	and the toolbar are ordinary systems registered alongside the game's,
505	made inert while Playing by an Edit guard (the transport chrome —
506	toolbar transport buttons + systems panel — deliberately stays live in
507	both states). There is no parallel editor data model: a scene
508	round-trips by serializing the entities' components, not by re-running
509	factories.
510	
511	**Key invariant — default `Play` + opt-in gating leaves every existing
512	screen byte-identical.** `RunMode` defaults to `Play`, and only a system
513	explicitly wrapped in a `GatedSystem` changes behavior with the mode. A
514	screen that never wraps a system and never sets `Edit` behaves exactly
515	as it did before the model existed. This is what makes the run-state
516	model safe to add across all modules at once.
517	
518	**Key rule — the gating policy per system group is fixed by what editing
519	needs to see and not disturb.** Render, input, cursor, and
520	`HierarchySystem` stay live in `Edit` (`RunNormally`) — the preview must
521	keep drawing, the designer must keep clicking, and an editor's transform
522	edit must still propagate to world space the same frame. Game logic,
523	physics, collision, AI/dialogue, and `CameraFollowSystem` `Freeze` in
524	`Edit` — they would otherwise move entities out from under the designer
525	or fight the editor for the camera; in `Edit` the editor drives
526	`Camera.Position`/`Zoom` directly. Get a policy wrong and the failure is
527	silent: a frozen render module is a black screen the instant you enter
528	`Edit`; a live physics module rains gravity on entities you are trying
529	to place; a frozen `HierarchySystem` shows edits at last frame's world
530	position. The authoritative system-by-mode table is the interaction
531	matrix in the level-editor plan-contract and
532	[`docs/flows/level-editor.md`](flows/level-editor.md); the run-state
533	premises live in
534	[`MonoDreams/foundation/docs/premises.md`](../MonoDreams/foundation/docs/premises.md).
535	
536	**Editor-overlay entities are standalone.** Gizmo handles, the selection
537	highlight, and the toolbar are never `ChildOfComponent`-parented to game
538	entities, because `HierarchySystem.DisposeOrphans` runs in `Edit` and
539	would cascade-dispose them when their host entity is deleted. Deletion is
540	modeled as an undo command that snapshots the disposed sub-graph, not a
541	bare `entity.Dispose()`.
542	
543	**The editor shell is a compositing concern, not a pipeline fork.** With
544	the editor composed, the game composite renders into a smaller centered
545	viewport (`ViewportManager.SetViewportInset` — deliberately the same
546	object that inverts the mouse mapping, so picking follows for free) and
547	the editor chrome renders around it at native window resolution
548	(`RenderTargetID.Editor` + `RenderLayer.Native`). The shell is
549	**constant across transport states** — it never collapses while Playing.
550	The game pipeline itself is untouched — same passes, same targets — and
551	without the run flag nothing editor-related is constructed: zero inset,
552	no chrome layer, byte-identical to a screen without the editor. Details:
553	the `rendering` and `level-editor` premises.
554	
555	**The editor is host- and screen-agnostic, and the pipeline is
556	inspectable.** The editor does not care which host or screen is running —
557	under the editor run flag every screen of every host (a menu or a module
558	demo as much as a level) builds its pipelines through the
559	`EditorPipelineRegistrar` and composes the `EditorOverlay` over its own
560	world, declaring its own per-system edit policies at the registration
561	site (e.g. a menu freezes its button interaction in `Edit` so clicks
562	belong to the editor; a runner freezes its whole simulation block). Where
563	a screen lacks a prerequisite, the overlay supplies it (its own cursor
564	pipeline for a cursor-less screen; the `DefaultEditorKeys` key surface
565	for a host with no action mapping) or degrades gracefully (no Y-sorted
566	layer ⇒ selection picks on the final source-derived depth). The recipe
567	for wiring a new host/screen is the level-editor overview's "Adding the
568	editor to a screen/host" section. The registrar
569	is also the live inspection surface — and it owns the hierarchy: composite
570	blocks are registrar groups (`AddGroup`) with named children, built and
571	gate-wrapped by the registrar itself (DefaultEcs composites hide their
572	children, so a screen must never pre-build an opaque composite for
573	anything it wants inspectable). The editor's systems panel renders that
574	tree — every entry of both pipelines, groups indented above their
575	children, name, policy, enabled state (tri-state on groups: all/none/
576	mixed) — and toggles any of them at runtime through `SetEnabled` (leaf =
577	both-modes master switch; group = cascade over its descendant leaves), so
578	the per-system edit-mode declaration is visible and adjustable while the
579	game runs.
580	
581	**Editing produces versioned, portable, diffable levels — the persistence
582	story.** A level the editor authors is saved as a native `.mdscene` **into
583	the game's SOURCE content tree** (`Content/Levels/<id>.mdscene`), versioned
584	in git — not into the ephemeral build output. Writing is a **desktop-dev-only**
585	capability (guarded by the editor run flag + an OS check + a resolved project
586	root, resolved via `MONODREAMS_PROJECT_ROOT` or a walk-up to the `game.mdproj`
587	manifest; unresolved disables Save loudly, never crashes); **reading is
588	console-portable** — the shipped game boots a level read-only through
589	`TitleContainer` over MGCB-`/copy:`-bundled files on every platform (desktop,
590	web, consoles), native-first via `LoadLevelRequest` (§6), so straying from
591	MGCB never costs console support. The serializer is **canonical and
592	byte-stable** (deterministic bytes, stable per-entity ids ordering
593	`entities[]`), so `load → edit → save` is a fixed point and a git diff of a
594	level is meaningful. A **`game.mdproj` manifest** makes "a MonoDreams project"
595	a versionable unit (entry scene, levels dir, asset roots). A new level bundles
596	**zero-touch** — the editor appends the MGCB `/copy:` entry on first save
597	(MGCB has no glob; a build-time regen would sweep gitignored placeholder art),
598	so it boots after a normal build with no manual `.mgcb` editing. And a scene is
599	**ship-ready** (fully portable) exactly when it has **zero `file:` AssetKeys** —
600	a checkable lint (all drop-folder art graduated to MGCB content keys); the
601	committed reference levels are asserted ship-clean. The invariants live in the
602	`level-editor` and `level-loading` premises.
603	
604	**One data model — anything authored is component state on an entity,
605	singletons included; special file blocks are debt.** A scene is a set of
606	entities carrying components, and *everything the designer authors lives that
607	way* — including the singletons it is tempting to model as a special
608	top-level file block (the scene camera, and later the layer map). A `camera`
609	block, a materialized editor rig for it, bespoke edit commands, and per-mode
610	re-sync seams are **four parallel representations of one value**, and every
611	one is a place the value can silently disagree with the others. The camera is
612	the case study: three camera defects in three days (zoom edits not reaching
613	the rig or the file) all lived in that camera-only plumbing; the day the
614	camera became an ordinary `core.Camera` entity — `EntityInfoComponent("Camera")`
615	+ `TransformComponent` (one rotation, on the Transform) + `CameraComponent`
616	zoom, serialized in `entities[]` like everything else — the block, the rig,
617	the commands, and the re-sync seams all deleted, exactly as colliders stopped
618	breaking the day they became child entities (§5).
619	
620	**Corollary — Inspector-visible ⇒ Save-persisted ⇒ round-trip-owned.** If a
621	value shows up in the Inspector, Save must persist it; if Save persists it,
622	`load → save` must own it as a byte fixed point. A value that is editable but
623	not serialized (or serialized but not round-trip-stable) is a bug waiting to
624	surface as "my edit vanished on reload". The one data model is what makes this
625	hold for free: an authored value is a component, and components already
626	round-trip.
627	
628	**The extension recipe (how to add a new authored thing).** Do NOT add a file
629	block or a bespoke editor subsystem. Instead:
630	
631	1. **Define a component** with clearly named authored vs derived fields (author
632	   the source; recompute the derived — e.g. `CameraComponent.Zoom` is authored,
633	   the view matrix is derived; a collider's `Size` is authored, its world AABB
634	   derived).
635	2. **Register its serializer** (`ComponentSerializerRegistry` — engine types in
636	   `EngineComponentSerializers`, game types in the game's own registration),
637	   so it round-trips through the canonical serializer.
638	3. **Optionally add an Inspector default-initializer** so "Add ⟨component⟩"
639	   births a sane instance.
640	
641	Those three steps buy the whole authoring stack — file authoring, Inspector
642	editing, undo, dirty-tracking, prefab overrides, byte-stable diffs, and
643	Game-mode sandbox protection — **by composition, not configuration**. There is
644	no fourth step and no special case. When a value seems to *need* a file block,
645	that is the signal it wants to be a component on an entity instead. (A legacy
646	block that predates this tenet is migrated forward by the CLI umbrella
647	`monodreams migrate` — the camera block's v2→v3 lift is the reference; see the
648	`level-editor` migrator premises.)
649	
650	### Aspirational direction
651	
652	The reserved `RunPartial` / `RuntimeEditable` policies are placeholders
653	for finer edit-time behavior (a system that does reduced work, or stays
654	interactive, while editing) — they run-as-`RunNormally` today and gain
655	distinct semantics when a later wave needs them. The interaction matrix
656	is enforced by review and by the editor screen's own tests until a
657	declarative system-dependency API (§2, §7) can validate it at
658	registration time.
659	
660	## 10. Refactor backlog (named cruft)
661	
662	Carried forward from the bootstrap interview so they are not forgotten.
663	Each is either implementation debt or an aspirational direction that
664	will eventually move from "documented in CORE_TENETS" to "enforced in
665	code".
666	
667	- **`ChildOf` vs `Transform.Parent` split** (§3). Two parent links
668	  exist today; consolidation desired. Until then, read both when
669	  reasoning about hierarchy.
670	- **`Visible` as a tag** (§4). Could become `DrawComponent.Visible`.
671	  Open question: would moving it complicate the bulk add/remove
672	  pattern `CullingSystem` uses today?
673	- **`Blender_` identifier prefix / parser-asymmetry** (§6). **RESOLVED
674	  (PS5); Blender importer DELETED (wave BR).** The game boot is a single
675	  native-only dispatcher (`LevelLoadRequestSystem`): `LoadLevelRequest` →
676	  native `.mdscene` via `SceneReaderSystem`, or fail loud. The LDtk module is
677	  import-only machinery (its own `LDtkLevelLoadSystem` + parsers, composed only
678	  in the reference screen's `importMode`, run by the export op), so nothing
679	  legacy runs at boot — and since issue #54 `level-loading` carries no LDtk
680	  type at all, so the separation is structural, not a flag. The
681	  Blender importer that once shared the `Blender_` name-prefix dispatch was
682	  retired wholesale in wave BR (parser + data types + exporter plugin + CLI
683	  registry entry + module-count docs), so the name-prefix hack is gone
684	  end-to-end — no parser asymmetry remains. Residual: the LDtk `Level_0` is
685	  not yet migrated to native (it needs a **native tile-layer batching
686	  primitive** — a compact representation for ~21k per-tile entities, so its
687	  `.mdscene` isn't a multi-MB per-entity dump); until then it is import-only
688	  and not offered by the reference menu. When the LDtk parser too is
689	  eventually deleted, the import op moves to a standalone tool.
690	- **`EntitySpawnSystem` silent-drops unregistered factories** (§6).
691	  Intended behaviour is to throw.
692	- **`Transform.Delta` consistency not enforced** (§3). No API today
693	  prevents reading stale `Delta` mid-frame; `Transform` should expose
694	  interaction methods that guarantee consistency.
695	- **Module-level coupling to `Transform`** (§3, §5). Collision,
696	  rendering, camera, culling all read `Transform` directly. The
697	  eventual end-state is loose coupling to any Transform-shaped
698	  contract.
699	- **Folder layout** (`Component/<subdomain>/` vs `Component/<file>/`
700	  inconsistency). Intended end-state is **modular packs** (Spring Data
701	  / Spring Security analog) — `MonoDreams.Rendering`,
702	  `MonoDreams.Physics`, etc. — that can be adopted independently.
703	- **Examples headless mode is logic-only** (§8). Its `Draw` early-returns,
704	  so it renders nothing — fine for replay/logic tests, useless for visual
705	  observation. The Demos headless path (issue #28) is the load-bearing
706	  observe-and-self-verify route and *does* render; the remaining debt is
707	  that the Examples mode is still named "headless" despite not rendering,
708	  and the two paths could eventually share one host abstraction.
709	- **No architectural tests** (§8). Most premises lack programmatic
710	  protection; review and discipline are the only enforcement today.
711	- **Declarative system dependencies** (§2, §7). A future API would let
712	  a system declare "I expect X to have run this frame" at registration
713	  time, replacing implicit-order discipline with explicit assertions.
714	- **Test or example per public contract** (§2). Several messages
715	  (`PositionChangeMessage`, `SizeChangeMessage`, `RigidBodyTouchMessage`)
716	  are exposed but may be leftovers without active consumers. Every
717	  contract should ship with at least one usage.
